Is Linux Still a Threat to Windows?

In the server market, absolutely. In the desktop market, not really. Linux has taken a huge market share of the server market by being low cost, scalable, reliable and customizable. Windows still has good market penetration though since it is better targeted at internal business operations and supports a wide range of hardware and software. Linux mostly shines for web use and applications targeting big data, crunching and distributed processing. Windows rules the desktop because it is easy to use, supports vast amounts of popular applications and hardware and has a polished UI/UX. Linus has been playing catch up to Windows in these areas throughout its history. So many Linux distros exist now making user choice too daunting and not suitable for long term adoption since no one distro has a reliable road map for long term development and support. Trendy distros come and go leaving adopters without a future when the bandwagon changes to the new popular distro. Linux also lacks enough polish and capability to attract hardware makers and business software developers. The terrible printing, audio and networking support in Linux will remain its obstacle to wider desktop adoption. The problem is drivers but the hardware makers rarely do anything to change this problem since there isn't enough incentive to support Linux. This prevents Linux from improving their hardware and subsystem capabilities which keeps the desktop market share from growing into the mainstream user. Business end users don't want to be messing around with configurations, distro changes, compiling software or scripting. They have jobs to do that don't involve them needing to be programmers, system admins or technicians. These users just want to use computers to improve their ability to do their primary job and not become computer savvy unless it's a hobby of theirs. Most don't have this as a hobby.

While I'd like to see Linux become a real challenger to Windows on the desktop, the reality is in the long history of Linux the dream has never been realized. It will take a lot of things to change for this to happen. Hardware and software makers will need to adopt Linux and to do so means Windows has to become less attractive to them. That's not happening any time soon even if Microsoft is making some critical missteps in how they evolve the Windows platform. The risk in going all Linux is too great for small businesses who just want to get things done and not become computer people in the process. This is something the Linux community seems to ignore since they would rather have everyone learn to be technical about computers. This needs to change before we can see Linux move forward into the mainstream of users and businesses.

The word processor needs to have full style control and formatting/layout with an extensible style library.
